newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Ikarus buses to Russia on $42m finance.
newsitem.headline: Ikarus buses to Russia on $42m finance.

text.p: An international bank consortium will help Hungarian busmaker Ikarus Jarmugyarto Rt rebuild its once formidable presence in Russia by providing $42.895 million to finance the sale of 403 buses to Moscow, the company said on Friday.

"This certainly is the biggest package of export finance for Ikarus this year, and it could be the largest ever," Ikarus chief executive Janos Gantner told Reuters, following a news conference about the loans.
Ikarus, which used to build over 10,000 buses a year in the 1980s, has drastically cut production since the collapse of its main market, the Soviet Union, in 1991.

The busmaker, under new management for a year, has started to turn around its business. Its output, which had fallen close to 1,500 units in 1996, is expected to top 2,000 in 1997, largely on the renewed strength of sales to Russia.
"This credit will help Ikarus to stand firmly on its feet again," Laszlo Madarasz, chief executive of BNP-Dresdner Bank (Hungaria) Rt, said at the news conference.

BNP-Dresdner, the consortium's lead manager, will lend 60 percent of the credit, while Central-European International Bank Ltd and the Hungarian Export-Import Bank will provide 20 percent each, bank officials said at the news conference.
Russian bank Rossiisky Kredit Bank will receive the funds and re-lend them to the Moscow city government, which in turn will buy the buses for a public transit company, bank officials said.
"This month, the first 80 buses can be delivered," Gantner said, noting that the credit contracts are for three years, and all buses will be delivered before December 1997.
Ikarus, which the Hungarian government plans to privatise this year, already has orders for 2,000 buses this year with nearly 70 percent coming from the former Soviet Union, he said.
The busmaker also is looking to export to new markets, especially Far East countries like Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam, Gantner said.
"In coming months, we will go to banks for new loans," he said at the news conference. "We are ready to export to other countries."

Ikarus also is rebuilding its presence in the former Soviet Union with Russian truckmaker AMO ZiL. The two companies have designed a minibus with an Ikarus body and ZiL chassis, and a prototype will be shown at the Moscow motor show in August, he told Reuters.
